extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Federal education funds (K-12 and postsecondary institutions), Title IX Coordinators, campus administrators, and their legal/compliance staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting and implementing the Title IX regulatory definitions of “complainant” and “complaint,” including who may be a complainant, timing of participation, allowable complaint formats (oral or written), and related recipient obligations (notice, recordkeeping, training, and supportive measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “complainant” — participation or attempting to participate (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of “complainant” in these final regulations shifts the focus of the analysis from whether the participation or attempted participation occurred at the time the complaint was filed to the time of the alleged sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether someone is participating or attempting to participate in a recipient's education program or activity requires a fact-specific analysis. The Department concluded that requiring participation or attempted participation at the time of the alleged discrimination is better aligned with Title IX's text and its goal because it addresses conduct that would have interfered with the complainant's ability to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be a complainant — includes some non-students/non-employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone who is not a student (or person authorized to act on behalf of a student) or an employee could still be a complainant if they were participating or attempting to participate in the recipient's education program or activity (e.g., a prospective student, a guest speaker, visiting student‑athlete, or attendees at campus events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The participation requirement is consistent with Federal appellate decisions (e.g., Doe v. Brown Univ.; Snyder‑Hill v. Ohio State Univ.) and is a fact-based determination depending on the reason for the visit and what the individual was doing at the time of the alleged discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not narrow “attempting to participate” to “applying”
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department does not agree that “applying” is a better way to describe “attempting to participate” because “applying” is too narrow in scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even someone who is not applying for admission might be participating or attempting to participate (e.g., visiting a campus, guest speaker). Use the broader participation/attempting-to-participate language rather than restricting to 'applying.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of participation requirement — limits recipients' legal obligation to initiate grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The participation requirement was added not to limit who can report sex discrimination or a recipient's obligation to respond promptly, but to prevent a recipient from being legally obligated to initiate its grievance procedures based on a complaint from a person having no relationship to the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between ability to report (anyone can report) and who qualifies as a complainant triggering grievance procedures (those with a connection via participation/attempted participation at time of alleged discrimination). The standard ensures the conduct could have 'excluded' the individual from participating or denied them educational benefits (20 U.S.C. 1681(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “complaint” — oral or written request objectively understood to request investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised the definition of a Title IX “complaint” to be an oral or written communication to the recipient that objectively can be understood as a request for the recipient to investigate and make a determination about alleged sex discrimination under Title IX and the relevant implementing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complainant need not use particular "magic words"; the test is whether a reasonable person could understand the communication as a request to investigate and make a determination. In general, this amounts to more than general questions about grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No written/signature requirement to commence investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require some form of written documentation of the complaint, short of the formal complaint requirement, to commence an investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients still have recordkeeping obligations (§106.8(f)), but exactly how to document complaints and actions is left to each recipient. Allowing oral complaints lowers barriers for complainants (age, disability, communication ability) and is intentional to facilitate reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive communication formats included in “oral or written”
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase “oral or written” is broad enough to include complaints made using most adaptive communication formats (e.g., sign language, physical gestures, drawings, communicating through an aide or caregiver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should not refuse to consider a complaint made using adaptive formats; if a complainant has a disability, Section 504 and the ADA still apply. The Department appreciated suggestions to specify facilitation but found explicit regulatory text unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the word “oral” (not “verbal”)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to change the word 'oral' to 'verbal' because 'oral' is commonly understood as spoken whereas 'verbal' can mean spoken or written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain 'oral' when referring to spoken complaints to preserve intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections to preserve integrity of investigations where complaint is oral
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department disagrees that oral complaints undermine investigation integrity; procedural protections in the grievance requirements (§106.45 and, if applicable, §106.46) are designed to protect the integrity of investigations and ensure a fair process for all parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protections include equal opportunity to access evidence, impartial decisionmakers, and other procedural safeguards. A written complaint may help but is neither necessary nor sufficient; recipients are responsible for following grievance procedures to ensure sound investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent notice requirement — recipients must provide sufficient notice (§106.45(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure a fair resolution, a recipient must provide a respondent with notice of the allegations against them sufficient for them to respond, which is required under final §106.45(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a complaint is oral or written, the recipient is responsible upon initiation of grievance procedures for providing sufficient notice. For student complainants/respondents at postsecondary institutions in sex‑based harassment cases, written notice is required by §106.46(c). See discussion of due process (Goss v. Lopez) for minimum expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant autonomy and initiation of grievance procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should generally not initiate grievance procedures if a complainant is not ready or does not want to initiate them, except when the Title IX Coordinator determines the conduct as alleged presents an imminent and serious threat to health or safety or prevents equal access under §106.44(f)(1)(v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title IX Coordinators should confirm complainant intent after explaining grievance procedures; the reasonable-person definition of 'complaint' helps mitigate misunderstandings. Title IX Coordinators may memorialize outcomes of conversations to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator duties on notification and confirmation (§106.44(f)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon being notified of conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination, the Title IX Coordinator must notify a complainant (or the individual who reported the conduct if complainant unknown) of the grievance procedures and, if applicable, the informal resolution process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During such conversations, the Coordinator will explain procedures and confirm whether the reporter wants an investigation. The Coordinator coordinates supportive measures and is not a confidential advisor; they should carefully confirm allegations and complainant intent and may memorialize decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-confidential employees' reporting duties (§106.44(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who are not confidential employees must notify the Title IX Coordinator of any information they have about conduct that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination, or provide a potential complainant with contact information for the Title IX Coordinator and information about how to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential complainants who want confidential support should seek out confidential employees where provided. Whether a conversation with a non-confidential employee constitutes a 'request to the recipient' is addressed elsewhere (§106.44(a) and (c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements and recipient discretion (§106.8(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.8(d)(4) requires that the Title IX Coordinator and any designees be trained on a number of specific topics and receive any other training necessary to coordinate the recipient's compliance; recipients have discretion over additional training content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to specify more than the required topics to balance necessary baseline training while allowing recipients flexibility to choose additional training relevant to their organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping obligations (§106.8(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.8(f) requires recipients to maintain (1) for each complaint of sex discrimination, records documenting the informal resolution process or the grievance procedures and resulting outcome, and (2) for each notification the Title IX Coordinator receives of information that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination, records documenting the actions the recipient took to meet obligations under §106.44.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exactly how to document information and steps taken is left to each recipient, but these recordkeeping obligations support accountability and help address disputes about whether a complaint was filed or how it was handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may not refuse complaints because they are not in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department does not think it appropriate to grant recipients discretion to deny a complaint because it was not submitted in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing recipients to require written-only complaints would recreate barriers the revised definition intends to remove; the goal is added flexibility for complainants and to avoid technicalities that discouraged reporting under the 2020 amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorializing oral complaints — allowed but not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the regulations do not require a complaint to be in writing, nothing prevents a complainant from memorializing their oral complaint in writing or confirming in writing that the recipient received their complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may also memorialize outcomes of conversations to avoid confusion. Recordkeeping requirements (§106.8(f)) and grievance procedure protections will help ensure sufficient information to initiate procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between OCR complaints (to Federal agency) and complaints to recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR's Case Processing Manual requires complaints filed with OCR to be in writing, but that is distinct from a complaint made to a recipient, which may be oral or written under these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An administrative complaint to OCR starts a federal process with wider consequences; a complaint to a recipient initiates internal processes which are time-sensitive and handled differently. Recipients should be aware of this distinction when responding or advising individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures and obligation to address sex discrimination even without formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Title IX and these regulations, a recipient with actual knowledge of possible sexual harassment (which can come from oral reports) is required to offer supportive measures to a complainant, with or without a formal complaint (§106.44(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging reporting and facilitating complaints is part of recipients' duty to effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate; while complaints may increase, recipients already have obligations to evaluate and address conduct reasonably constituting sex discrimination.
